title: Custom string concatenation
instructorPromptText: Write a C function `void custom_strcat(char *dest, const char *src)` that appends the source string to the destination string using pointers. Do not use any `<string.h>` library functions.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the program correctly traverse to the end of the destination string (`\0`) before starting the copy?
specGateDimensions.rationale: To concatenate, the writer must understand how C strings are null-terminated and how to advance pointers to that position.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the code strictly avoid using functions from `<string.h>` (like `strcat`, `strcpy`, or `strlen`)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Writing manual string operations reinforces character-by-character pointer arithmetic and dereferencing.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the function explicitly place a null terminator (`\0`) at the final position of the destination string?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Forgetting the null terminator is a classic C bug that leads to garbage printing or memory access bugs.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student includes `<string.h>` and calls standard library functions like `strcat`.
Student forgets to null-terminate the final combined string in the destination buffer.
Student overwrites the destination string from the beginning instead of finding the end first.
Student uses a single compact while loop expression like `while (*dest++);` and needs to adjust for overshoot.
Student dereferences `dest` or `src` without checking if they are NULL, risking segmentation fault.
